newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Noblewoman's manor triumph celebrates 400 years.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Noblewoman's manor triumph celebrates 400 years.

text.p: Her life had all the makings of a Hollywood drama: sex, power, money, and intrigue.

The Countess of Shrewsbury was a woman distinctly ahead of her time -- a small town girl who made it big. She married four times, each husband more powerful and wealthier than the last, and outlived them all.
Bess of Hardwick, as she is better known, rose to become the second most powerful woman in Tudor England after Queen Elizabeth I.
And nothing embodies the tenacious spirit of this 16th century noblewoman more than Hardwick Hall, the manor she built for herself which is currently celebrating its 400th anniversary.
THE HOUSE THAT BESS BUILT
Erected by the unconventional Bess after being chased from her nearby estate by her estranged husband, the powerful Earl of Shrewsbury, Hardwick Hall also defied convention.
It has been called a 'petrified butterfly' and after 400 years of the harsh northern English climate the house suffers from severe decay, but it has retained all its original grace.
At a time when many manor houses remained forbidding stone behemoths, Hardwick radiated with splendour and light.

The visitor is immediately struck by the golden hue of its masonry and the enormous windows -- 186 in all, running to one-and-a-quarter acres of glass. "Hardwick Hall, more glass than wall," ran a contemporary jingle.

But the most imposing feature, and perhaps the clearest indication of Bess's unbridled ambitions, comes as the eyes lift towards the sky. The letters "ES" -- for Elizabeth of Shrewsbury -- topped by a crown elaborately, almost arrogantly, adorn each of the house's turrets.
Bess's new home took nearly 12 years to complete. During its construction she lived in the crumbling manor house where she grew up, just several hundred yards from her future mansion.

On October 4, 1597 at the age of 70 she moved into an uncompleted Hardwick Hall. It was not a grand entrance. "She came with a few musicians and a box of dried fish," said estate manager Chris Corry-Thomas.
Bess spent lavishly on the house's decor and in 1601 compiled a detailed inventory of the contents for her will. Many of the objects she meticulously recorded still adorn the ageing halls.
But the house's beauty did not come without a price. The lavish windows often meant severe cold inside, which Bess tried to ward off by leaving hardly a trace of bare wood or stone uncovered.
Tapestries adorn nearly every wall and rich fabrics -- from gold and silver cloth to silk damask, velvet and satins -- cover almost everything else.
A WOMAN OF INDEPENDENT MEANS
Bess sought nothing less than to establish a personal dynasty and her new home was to be the personification of her power and wealth.

Born in 1527 plain Elizabeth Hardwick was the daughter of a humble country squire. She died a countess in 1608 at the age of 80, owning more than 100,000 acres (40,000 hectares) of land with an annual income of 10,000 pounds -- a very substantial fortune in today's terms.
In addition to her vast real estate holdings, she operated quarries and lead and iron furnaces that supplied many of the estates in the area.
"She was an early industrialist really," said Corry-Thomas. "But after eight years here I'm still trying to understand just what kind of a woman she was."
As a controversial and much-feared figure she attracted both admirers and her enemies, but few could ignore her.

"A woman of masculine understanding and conduct, proud, furious, selfish and unfeeling. She was a builder, a buyer and seller of estates, a moneylender, a farmer and a merchant of lead, coals and timber; when disengaged from those employments, she intrigued alternately with (Queen) Elizabeth and Mary (Queen of Scots), always to the prejudice and terror of her husband," wrote Edmund Lodge in his "Illustrations of British History" in 1790.

The queen appointed Bess the official gaoler of Mary Queen of Scots, who stayed with her for nearly 15 years. The two of them spent countless hours together working on much of Hardwick's elaborate embroidery.
A BATTLE AGAINST THE ELEMENTS

Hardwick has suffered severely since those days and presents enormous challenges to the caretakers trying to preserve it. Particularly threatened are the vast array of textiles, a collection unrivalled in Europe.

The light that makes the hall so splendid has contributed greatly to its deterioration. The constant bombardment of the sun's rays has badly faded the tapestries and rendered them brittle and very fragile.

"Light is our most precious commodity," says Corry-Thomas as he walks among the house's darkened chambers. "We're only permitted to allow in 1,000 hours of daylight all year," he explains. "It is just too harmful."
Each tapestry requires between 2,000 and 3,000 hours to conserve, with the bill for the rarest 13 estimated at 1.5 million pounds ($2.5 million).

Water from the region's near constant rainfall streams through the windows where the leaded panes have slipped and worn away over the centuries. Acidity in the air and rain slowly eats away at the soft masonry from the estate's quarries.

Britain's National Trust, which has owned the manor since the Duke of Devonshire passed it to the state in 1959 in lieu of inheritance taxes, estimates that nearly 18 million pounds are needed for essential repairs.
The most pressing priorities are replacing the decaying exterior stone and restoring the tapestries.
Seven full-time masons work at Hardwick using stone still quarried on the estate. They have used nearly 1,600 tonnes of it since restoration began in 1985.
Visitors to the home pose a particular dilemma because their ticket money brings in desperately needed resources, but their very presence weighs heavily on the creaking home.

"The breathing, touching, stepping, even sweating can cause terrible damage," says Corry-Thomas. "But Hardwick belongs to the nation. If the public cannot come here and enjoy it, then what's the point of preserving it at all?"
Besides, he concludes, "Bess might have rather enjoyed all the attention." ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
